title: Family practice network: systematic review of continuity and unplanned admissions, a failed search, leads only, then two hits
notes: Ordinary path with a search that finds little. The need names a systematic review (routing explicit). The first recorded search fails with HTTP 500: the retrieval event is 'error' with resultCount null and no records, visible rather than silently empty. The scan reply that follows (shape discovery) offers five model leads, one labelled 'landmark', and no certainty: the leads are stored as unverified model leads whatever their label (G3), and the stage stays incomplete, shown as leads only and not assessed (G1, G2; D20). A reworded second search returns only two hits; both records are appended after the leads, and the appraisal (S13) over them records two claims and certainty 'very-low' (two observational studies, one compatible with no change). The stage completes only now. The decision to run the full review rests on c1 and c2, and its single gate (protected reviewer time) is met on the committee minute, so the accepted action is ready. The two-record search is below the usual 5 to 9 records because thin evidence is the point of the scenario. Record ids are stableRecordId(record) from src/lib/evidence/records.ts at 875fe59, computed by the generator script: 'ev-' plus the base-36 FNV-1a hash of the normalised DOI (records 1 ev-1fh7abw), or of titleYearKey(title, year) when there is no DOI (records 2 ev-0ygi9te). Catches: a failed search reported as an empty or successful one, a 'landmark' label turned into verification, completion or certainty from leads, and over-confident certainty from two records.

inputs.need:
I chair the quality committee of the Kestrel Valley Family Practice Network, nine practices with 38 family physicians. Over the last five years our older patients have increasingly been booked with whichever physician is free, and several of us believe that losing the relationship with a usual physician is part of why our patients over 65 are admitted to hospital more often than they used to be. The network is considering reorganising appointments so that patients aged 65 and over see their own physician for most visits, which would lengthen waits for some people.

Before we reorganise, I want a systematic review of whether higher continuity of care with a family physician is associated with fewer unplanned hospital admissions among older adults. I expect the evidence is mostly observational, uses different continuity indices, and comes from health systems that may not resemble ours. I would like the review to tell us how large the association is, whether it holds after accounting for how sick people are, and whether any study changed continuity on purpose and measured admissions afterwards.

Two colleagues and a nurse practitioner are willing to help, and the committee has agreed to protect some of our time this winter. I need help with a focused question, sensible inclusion criteria, which continuity measures to accept, how to deal with confounding by illness severity in the included studies, and whether pooling is realistic.
inputs.constraints: Three reviewers (two physicians and a nurse practitioner) with about 40 hours each from October 2026 to March 2027. No funding. Studies from primary care in high-income health systems, published in English.
localFacts: The network has nine practices, 38 family physicians and about 61,000 registered patients, 11,900 of them aged 65 or over.

records.title: Continuity with a usual family physician and unplanned hospital admission in adults aged 65 and over: a population study
records.authors: Engelbrecht-Musa R, Holloway-Nakata S, Pereira-Achebe L
records.abstract: We followed 118,000 adults aged 65 and over registered with family practices for two years, measuring continuity with a usual provider index from outpatient visits in the first year. Patients in the highest continuity quintile had fewer unplanned admissions in the second year than those in the lowest (rate ratio 0.84, 95 percent CI 0.79 to 0.90) after adjustment for age, sex, number of chronic conditions and prior admissions. The association was stronger for admissions for ambulatory care-sensitive conditions (rate ratio 0.76). Sicker patients see more physicians, so residual confounding by severity is possible despite adjustment.

records.title: Changes in continuity after practice reorganisation and emergency admissions: an interrupted time series in 14 practices
records.abstract: Fourteen family practices introduced personal lists that linked each patient aged 65 and over to one physician. Over 18 months, the continuity index for these patients rose from 0.46 to 0.61. Emergency admissions among them fell by 6 percent relative to the pre-existing trend (95 percent CI -1 to 12 percent), an estimate compatible with no change. Waits for routine appointments rose from a median of 6 to 9 days. There were no comparison practices, and a regional admission avoidance scheme started during the same period.

steps.note: Reworded second search: only two hits, both with abstracts, appended after the five leads. Ids are stableRecordId values (see notes).

response.synthesis: Two retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. A large population study found fewer unplanned admissions with higher continuity among older adults after adjustment, strongest for ambulatory care-sensitive conditions, but residual confounding by severity is likely. The only study that raised continuity deliberately found an admissions change compatible with no effect and longer waits. Two records cannot answer the question; they justify a full systematic search.
response.gradeRationale: Two observational studies, one uncontrolled with an imprecise estimate; serious risk of confounding and imprecision.
response.summary: Two retrieved records appraised; two claims recorded; overall certainty very low.

steps.note: The appraisal applies to the two retrieved records only (S13); the leads stay unverified. Certainty is assigned now, over inspected records (G1), and the stage completes because records were retrieved (G2).

response.reading: Continuity may reduce admissions by letting a physician notice deterioration and manage chronic conditions early, which is why the association is strongest for ambulatory care-sensitive conditions. But sicker patients see more physicians, so severity drives both low continuity and admissions. The single reorganisation study suggests that raising continuity deliberately costs waiting time and may not change admissions quickly.

response.rationale: A systematic review answers the network's question better than a local analysis, which could not separate continuity from severity with nine practices. The preliminary search found an adjusted association (c1) and one intervention study with an imprecise result (c2); a full search is needed because two records cannot settle the question. Studies must adjust for severity to be pooled, and intervention studies are reported separately.

response.overview: Systematic review of observational and intervention studies of relational continuity with a family physician and unplanned hospital admissions in adults aged 65 and over.

response.procedures: Search three bibliographic databases from 2000, with forward citation checking of included studies and a check of every scan lead. response.title: Relational continuity with a family physician and unplanned admissions in older adults: a systematic review
response.abstract: Objective: to estimate the association between relational continuity with a family physician and unplanned admissions in adults aged 65 and over, in studies that adjust for illness severity, and the effect of interventions designed to raise continuity. Methods: systematic review with severity-adjusted pooling and intervention studies reported separately. Results will follow the full search.
response.introduction: Continuity is valued by patients and physicians, and several studies link it to fewer admissions. Because sicker patients see more physicians, unadjusted associations overstate any benefit, and few studies have raised continuity on purpose.
response.methods: Three bibliographic databases are searched from 2000 with forward citation checking, and every lead from the preliminary scan is checked. Two reviewers screen independently and a third resolves disagreements. Only estimates adjusted for morbidity or prior use are pooled; intervention studies and waiting times are tabulated separately.
response.results: The full search has not been run; the preliminary search returned two records.
response.discussion: To be written against the network's decision on personal lists. The discussion will weigh any association against the waiting-time cost shown by intervention studies.
response.limitations: English-language studies from high-income systems only; residual confounding by severity in included studies.

Search for an existing severity-adjusted review (defeating criterion k2 is unknown)
response.improvementNotes: The first search failed and the second returned two records; certainty is very low and rests on those two records only. The leads remain unverified.
response.summary: Three open fixes; the full search comes next.
